P-001.author: researcher-mathematical
P-001.title: Smooth, injective inverse map on the compact prior box: a direct learned inverse (log-target MLP) reaches rel_l2 < 0.05
P-001.hypothesis: The discrete forward map F: k in [0.5,2]^4 -> R^{4xT} (explicit FD, 40 nodes, 200 steps) is C-infinity in k. Its Jacobian has full column rank 4 everywhere on the box, so F is injective with a Lipschitz inverse on F(box). A direct regressor X -> log k with enough capacity therefore approaches the noise-limited error. Because sigma = 1e-3 is small relative to the sensor signal, that error floor is well below 0.05. The main obstacle is approximation error, not ill-posedness. Error will be anisotropic: k1 and k4 have larger errors than k2 and k3, because the pulse starts at x = 0.5 and reaches the outer segments late and with low amplitude.
P-001.motivation: Sensors at grid indices 5, 15, 25, 35 sit inside each of the four segments, so every k_i directly controls local diffusion at a sensor. The pulse is symmetric about x = 0.5, but the k values are not symmetric, and the outflow to the Dirichlet ends couples k1 and k4 into all four time series. With 4 parameters and roughly 800 noisy observations, a Gauss-Newton count (4x4 Fisher matrix J^T J / sigma^2) predicts a small Cramér-Rao bound unless J is nearly rank-deficient. A log-target parameterisation matches the multiplicative way k enters the diffusion time scale (t ~ L^2/k), which linearises the map. The mean baseline of 0.33 leaves a wide margin.
assumptions: Segments are the four equal quarters of [0,1], each containing exactly one sensor.
The training data are generated by the same simulator and noise model as val and test (sigma = 0.001, i.i.d.).
Sensitivities dF/dk_i are not near-collinear anywhere in the box (local identifiability), which is a conjecture rather than a proven fact.
noise_scale is interpreted in raw feature units. If it is in scaled units, the augmentation is a negligible jitter and is harmless.

evidence.claim: The forward problem is well-posed, so F is a single-valued map of k. This says nothing about the inverse.

Uniqueness results for identifying a spacewise diffusion coefficient exist for the heat equation. However, they assume regular coefficients and final-time full-field data, unlike our piecewise-constant k and 4 point sensors.

Four scalar unknowns against roughly 4xT observations is a heavily overdetermined, finite-dimensional problem. Finite-dimensional parameterisation regularises the usual exponential ill-posedness of parabolic coefficient inversion.

The outer segments receive heat only after diffusion through the inner segments and lose it to the zero-Dirichlet ends. Sensitivity to k1 and k4 may therefore be weak, which would inflate their error.

citations.note: Gives uniqueness of the forward solution for positive integrable A. Stated on R^n in L^2, not on [0,1] with Dirichlet ends. It supports only that F is well defined, not invertibility.

Same equation class. Its assumptions fail here: it needs a regular coefficient (ours is discontinuous) and final-time spatial data (ours is 4 point sensors over time). It is used only as motivation that spacewise k can be identifiable.

P-001.falsifiable_test: The test fails if val rel_l2 is at or above 0.05. A secondary check: if per-parameter val RMSE for k1 and k4 is not larger than for k2 and k3, the anisotropic-sensitivity claim is falsified.

feasibility.notes: 3000 x roughly 800 features, CPU MLP, 300 epochs with early stopping. Expected well under 120 s.

P-001.if_fails: If the error saturates above 0.05 and concentrates in k1 and k4, the outer conductivities are practically non-identifiable at sigma = 1e-3. In that case the posterior-mean estimate (shrinking toward 1.25) is the right target, not a sharper regressor. If the error is uniform, the bottleneck is approximation or sample size, which points to the surrogate-inversion proposal.

P-002.author: researcher-mathematical
P-002.title: Learned forward surrogate + per-sample weighted least-squares inversion beats the direct inverse regressor
P-002.hypothesis: The forward map k -> u(sensors, t) is a smooth map from a low-dimensional input (4-D) to a high-dimensional output. It is easier to learn than the inverse map, which must also average out the noise in 800 input dimensions. Training an MLP surrogate g of the forward map on the training pairs, then solving min_s ||W(g(s) - x)||^2 per sample, should reduce val rel_l2 by at least 15% relative to the best direct regressor. Here s is mapped into the box by tanh, W rescales residuals to raw units (the MLE under i.i.d. Gaussian noise), and the solve is warm-started from a learned inverse net. The method keeps whichever of init and refined does better on an internal 10% hold-out, so it cannot be worse than its own initializer by construction.
P-002.motivation: This is the analytical-inversion route: Levenberg-Marquardt-style MLE through F, which the harness cannot run because F is unavailable. It is replaced by a learned F that uses only simulated training data, which is allowed. The forward net exploits the known noise model, while a direct regressor learns the noise model only implicitly. Bounded tanh reparameterisation enforces the positivity and box constraints exactly. If ||g - F|| is well below the noise level, the estimator inherits the near-efficiency of the MLE.
assumptions: The surrogate's approximation error in raw units can be pushed to roughly 1e-3 or below with 2700 training pairs. This is the critical, falsifiable assumption.
The least-squares landscape is locally convex around the learned initializer, so first-order steps (Adam on tanh-parameterised s) converge in 150 steps.
Segment bounds are hard-coded as [0.5, 2.0], matching the stated prior, so the context object is not used.
uses_forward = false: no calls to the unavailable simulator.

evidence.claim: In finite-dimensional parameter estimation with a correct forward model and Gaussian noise, the MLE is asymptotically efficient. A direct regressor's accuracy is instead limited by how well it learns the inverse.
A forward map from 4 inputs to many outputs is smooth and low-intrinsic-dimension, which favours accurate surrogate regression.
If the surrogate error exceeds sigma, refinement fits surrogate artefacts and can degrade estimates. The hold-out gate exists for this reason.

citations.note: Only supports that the forward solution is unique for positive k, so a forward surrogate targets a well-defined function. The domain and boundary assumptions differ (R^n vs [0,1] Dirichlet).

P-002.falsifiable_test: The test fails if val rel_l2 is not at least 15% lower than the best direct data-driven model (e.g. the proposal-1 MLP). It also fails if the internal gate selects the un-refined initializer (use = False), which would show that the surrogate error exceeds the noise level.

feasibility.notes: Two 3000-step minibatch MLP trainings (about 10-30 s each on CPU at D of roughly 800). The batched 150-step refinement over 750 samples is cheap. It should fit within the 120 s per-experiment limit; if D is much larger, steps can be reduced.

P-002.if_fails: If refinement does not help, the learned forward map is not accurate to within the noise level at this sample size, so surrogate-MLE offers no advantage over amortised inversion. Effort should then go into ensembling or posterior-mean shrinkage. If it helps on k2 and k3 but not on k1 and k4, that confirms weak outer-segment sensitivity, meaning the Fisher information is ill-conditioned in the k1 and k4 directions.

P-003.author: researcher-ml
P-003.title: Noise-augmented MLP on standardized raw sensor traces, predicting log-conductivity
P-003.hypothesis: The map from sensor traces to k is smooth and has only 4 degrees of freedom, and the noise is small (sigma = 0.001). So an MLP should learn it well from 3000 samples. Train it on standardized raw traces, predict log k, and augment the inputs with Gaussian noise at the true sigma. Expected result: val rel_l2 <= 0.05, about 6x better than the mean predictor (0.33).
P-003.motivation: There is no forward model, so only learned inverse maps are possible. The prior box [0.5, 2] spans a factor of 4, so log k evens out the scale of the errors. The main risk is k1 and k4: their segments sit next to the Dirichlet ends, so less heat from the centred pulse reaches them, the sensitivity is lower and those components may be weakly identified. Adding noise at the true sigma acts as a regularizer that matches the noise model, so the network cannot rely on directions in the data that are too small to survive the noise.
assumptions: The features are the sensor time series, roughly 4 sensors by a set of time steps, and the noise is i.i.d. N(0, 0.001^2)
The 3000 simulated training samples cover the 4-D uniform prior densely enough for a smooth interpolant (about 7 points per axis)

The parameters are locally identifiable from four interior sensors. This is not proved here; it rests on reasoning only, because the retrieved stability results assume smooth coefficients or different boundary conditions
The temperatures stay large compared with sigma at the sensors near the ends during the time window

evidence.claim: The mean predictor gives 0.3307, so the targets have high variance across the prior; 0.05 needs about a 6.6x reduction

Lipschitz stability of a parabolic coefficient-recovery problem near a reference parameter would make the inverse map smooth enough to learn; but this was shown for a Robin coefficient with Neumann/Robin data, not here
Segments 1 and 4 are next to zero-Dirichlet ends, so their sensitivity may be much weaker than for k2 and k3, which could keep the overall rel_l2 above 0.05

citations.note: Parabolic equation and a quantitative stability statement both match. It assumes a Robin coefficient, Neumann/Robin boundaries and a positivity condition on the boundary; our problem has piecewise-constant interior k and Dirichlet ends. I use it only as an analogy for local Lipschitz stability, not as a proof.
Gives uniqueness of a 1-D L^inf conductivity, but from final-time full-space data plus a source term. We have point sensors over time, so it does not transfer directly.

P-003.falsifiable_test: Train on the train split and report val rel_l2 overall and per component. The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 > 0.05. If the per-component errors for k1 and k4 exceed 2x those for k2 and k3, the failure comes from weak identifiability near the ends, not from model capacity.

feasibility.notes: 3000 samples, a small MLP, CPU only: about 30-60 s, within the 120 s per-experiment limit.

P-003.if_fails: If val error is near train error, the limit is irreducible ambiguity, meaning k1 and k4 are poorly identified, and the posterior is wide. If train error is far below val error, the model is overfitting; then try a larger noise_aug, PCA compression or ensembling.

P-004.author: researcher-ml
P-004.title: Kernel ridge on PCA-compressed traces with log targets: a low-dimensional smooth-manifold estimator
P-004.hypothesis: The noise-free traces lie on a smooth 4-D manifold. The leading 20-30 principal components should capture nearly all of the variation that depends on k, and the rest should be close to noise (sigma = 0.001). If so, RBF kernel ridge on 24 PCA components predicting log k should match or beat the MLP, reaching val rel_l2 < 0.05 with fewer tuning choices.
P-004.motivation: With only 4 parameters and 3000 samples, a well-tuned RBF smoother works like a Gaussian-process regressor. It is close to optimal for smooth maps at this sample density, and it fits in seconds. PCA removes noise-dominated directions before the isotropic RBF distance, which otherwise weights them equally. If the kernel model matches the MLP, then the architecture is not the bottleneck, and remaining error is about information content or sample density.
assumptions: The trace manifold is well captured by about 24 linear principal components
An isotropic RBF on standardized PCA scores is an adequate metric; the components are not standardized to whiten noise directions
3000x3000 kernel memory is fine on CPU

evidence.claim: A 4-parameter smooth forward map makes the data intrinsically 4-D. Kernel methods converge quickly in low intrinsic dimension
The default 'scale' bandwidth may be badly mismatched after PCA. The default alpha=0.01 may oversmooth at this high SNR

citations.note: Allows non-smooth coefficients and gives stability, but for elliptic equations with internal (full-field) data. We have sparse point sensors, so it is only weak motivation for a well-posed smooth inverse map.

P-004.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 with the MLP from proposal 1. The hypothesis is falsified if KRR val rel_l2 > 0.05, or if it is more than 1.3x worse than the MLP. If it beats or matches the MLP, the PCA compression and smooth-interpolation assumption is confirmed.

feasibility.notes: PCA plus a 3000x3000 kernel solve takes a few seconds; a small alpha/gamma sweep also fits in the budget.

P-004.if_fails: If KRR loses badly to the MLP, the inverse map has a scale that varies across the prior, for example sharper behaviour at low k, so a single bandwidth cannot fit it. That favours adaptive models such as MLPs or ensembles. If both methods plateau at the same error, the limit is identifiability, not the estimator.

P-005.author: researcher-experimental
P-005.title: Noise-matched, log-target torch MLP: is the inverse map smooth enough at sigma=0.001 that a learned regressor reaches rel_l2 <= 0.05?
P-005.hypothesis: With one sensor centred in each conductivity segment (grid indices 5,15,25,35 of 40), each k_i has a distinct signature in the sensor time series. The signal-to-noise ratio at sigma=0.001 is high, so the data-to-k map is a smooth, well-conditioned function on the prior box. A standardized-feature MLP trained on log(k) with Gaussian noise augmentation should therefore reach val rel_l2 < 0.05. We also predict that the residual error is not uniform across segments: k1 and k4 will have higher error than k2 and k3. Those outer segments receive heat later and with lower amplitude from the centred pulse, and Dirichlet sinks at the ends further reduce their sensitivity.
P-005.motivation: The forward model is unavailable, so only amortized data-driven inversion is executable. The prior is a 4-D box, and 3000 training samples is dense coverage for 4 parameters if the map is smooth. That favours a flexible smooth regressor over trees. Trees are piecewise-constant in feature space and waste capacity on 800-ish correlated time samples. A log target matches the multiplicative scale of conductivity and enforces positivity. Noise augmentation enlarges the effective training set without changing the measurement distribution, because test noise is the same i.i.d. Gaussian. The per-segment error breakdown is the measurement-design diagnostic: it tells us whether the remaining error is a capacity problem or an identifiability problem.
assumptions: Train, val and test are drawn from the same simulator, prior and noise distribution (i.i.d. uniform k, sigma=0.001), so there is no simulation-fidelity shift between splits.
The features are the raw noisy sensor time series (4 sensors x discrete times) without hidden normalization, so sigma=0.001 is on the same scale as the temperatures.
The harness applies noise_scale in raw feature units before scaling. If it applies it after standardization, the augmentation is effectively tiny, which is harmless.
The explicit FD simulator is stable (CFL satisfied at k=2.0), so no numerically corrupted samples exist in the training data.

evidence.claim: Mean predictor gives val rel_l2 0.3307, so reaching 0.05 needs roughly 6.6x error reduction. This is plausible for a 4-parameter smooth map at high SNR.
Sensor placement gives one interior observation per segment, so the Jacobian with respect to k should be close to full rank (block-diagonal-dominant).

Outer segments are far from the centred Gaussian pulse and adjacent to the Dirichlet sinks. Their temperature signal may stay close to the noise floor over the finite window, which could cap achievable accuracy for k1 and k4.
Uniqueness of spacewise diffusion coefficients for the heat equation has been shown under regularity and final-time-data assumptions. This is suggestive only, since those assumptions fail here.

citations.note: These assumptions hold: same parabolic divergence-form equation and a spacewise-only coefficient. These fail: the theorem assumes a regular coefficient (ours is discontinuous piecewise-constant), uses final-time full-spatial data (we have 4 point sensors over time), and identifies a source jointly. It motivates identifiability only heuristically and proves nothing about our 4-parameter, 4-sensor setup.

This is a Lipschitz stability result for continuation from the interior, not for coefficient identification. It hints that interior data can control the solution stably, but it does not bound how errors in k propagate. Not used as support for any quantitative claim.

P-005.falsifiable_test: The hypothesis is refuted if val rel_l2 >= 0.05. The secondary claim is refuted if the per-parameter relative errors for k1 and k4 are not larger than those for k2 and k3 (for example, all four within 10% of each other). Uniform errors would mean the bottleneck is regressor capacity or data size, not sensor sensitivity. Control: compare against ridge on the same features. If ridge is within 20% of the MLP, the map is near-linear and nonlinearity is not the issue.

feasibility.notes: 3000 x (about 800) features at 250 epochs on CPU should take about 30-60 s, within the 120 s per-experiment limit. Augmentation doubles the effective data size.

P-005.if_fails: If error is concentrated in k1 and k4, the outer segments are weakly observed in the finite time window. That is a measurement-design limit, and the next steps would be per-segment weighting, late-time or log/sqrt feature emphasis, or posterior-mean estimation to reduce MSE under the box prior. If errors are uniform, the problem is sample efficiency, and we should try kernel methods or PCA-denoised inputs.

P-006.author: researcher-experimental
P-006.title: Competing explanation: low-dimensional smooth manifold. PCA-denoised kernel ridge on sqrt features matches the MLP.
P-006.hypothesis: Parabolic smoothing forces the 4-sensor time series onto a low-dimensional manifold, with roughly 4 intrinsic dimensions plus noise. Projecting onto 20 leading PCA components removes most of the i.i.d. noise energy, which is spread across all features, while keeping the signal. An RBF kernel ridge regressor on that representation with a log target should then reach val rel_l2 < 0.06, within 1.25x of the best data-driven model. Applying a sqrt transform to the features compresses the dynamic range between the large central signals and the small outer-segment signals. This makes the isotropic RBF distance less dominated by sensors 2 and 3, and should reduce the k1 and k4 error compared with raw features.
P-006.motivation: This is a controlled, structurally different alternative to the MLP. It is a nonparametric smooth interpolant with an explicit noise-filtering front end. If it matches the MLP, the inverse map is essentially a smooth 4-D interpolation problem, and the scarce LLM and compute budget should go to denoising or feature design rather than network capacity. The sqrt transform is a measurement-scaling hypothesis: an isotropic kernel implicitly weights sensors by their variance, and the outer sensors carry less variance but are the only information about k1 and k4. Caveat: sqrt of values near zero corrupted by noise can be negative or ill-defined. The harness presumably handles this, for example with sign-preserving sqrt. If it does not, that failure is itself diagnostic.
assumptions: The noise-free sensor signals lie near a smooth 4-parameter manifold, so most signal variance is captured by the leading ~20 principal components.
The harness 'sqrt' feature set handles near-zero or negative noisy readings robustly, for example with sign(x)*sqrt(|x|).
3000 training points cover the 4-D prior box densely enough for an RBF interpolant, at roughly 7 points per axis-equivalent.
The same simulator and noise apply across all splits.

evidence.claim: The heat semigroup damps high spatial modes exponentially, so the sensor histories are highly correlated across time. This suggests a small effective dimension and makes PCA denoising effective against i.i.d. noise.

Kernel ridge with the 'scale' bandwidth heuristic can be badly mis-tuned on PCA features with very unequal variances. The default gamma_mult may underfit the low-variance components that encode k1 and k4.
Mean-baseline val rel_l2 of 0.3307 gives the reference scale for judging improvement.

citations.note: Aronson-type fundamental solution estimates require dimension >= 2 per the screen, a Lipschitz-in-x coefficient (ours is discontinuous), and random time dependence. It is cited only to record that the smoothing intuition is not formally covered by this result in our setting.
This gives heuristic identifiability support only. The regular-coefficient and final-time-data assumptions fail here, as noted in the first proposal.

P-006.falsifiable_test: The manifold hypothesis is refuted if val rel_l2 > 1.25x that of the noise-matched MLP, or if it is > 0.06 in absolute terms. The sqrt-scaling sub-hypothesis is refuted if the same configuration with features='raw' gives an equal or lower k1/k4 relative error. That would show dynamic-range compression is not what limits the outer segments. A third check: if the leading 20 PCA components explain < 99% of training feature variance, the low-dimensional-manifold assumption is wrong.

feasibility.notes: KRR on 3000 (or 6000 with augmentation) points: a 6000x6000 kernel takes about 290 MB and a solve takes a few seconds. PCA is cheap. Well within 120 s. The raw-feature ablation adds a second cheap run.

P-006.if_fails: If KRR clearly underperforms the MLP, the inverse map has anisotropic or non-stationary structure that an isotropic RBF on PCA coordinates cannot capture. That favours learned representations, for example an MLP, or custom per-target bandwidths. If sqrt does not help, outer-segment error is caused by limited information (sensitivity near the noise floor) rather than feature scaling, which points back to an identifiability limit and to MMSE-oriented estimators.

Diffusive time scales go as 1/k, so sensor responses depend roughly multiplicatively on k and the inverse map should be smoother and more uniformly conditioned in log space.
P-007.motivation: The default framing regresses k directly. For u_t=(k u_x)_x, scaling k on a segment rescales local diffusion time, so sensitivities dX/dk scale like 1/k. Low-k segments then get large-magnitude gradients and high-k segments flat ones. A log target equalises this. Noise augmentation at sigma=0.001 stops the network from exploiting sub-noise features that do not generalise. The prior is uniform in k, not log k, so this choice is a bias-variance trade we can test, not a free win.
assumptions: The harness target_transform='log' trains on log y and returns exp(prediction) in the original units
noise_scale is expressed in multiples of (or equal to) the stated sensor noise 0.001
The four segments are each informed by at least one of the sensors at indices 5, 15, 25, 35 (one sensor per segment if segments are equal quarters of 40 points)

P-016.author: researcher-experimental
P-016.title: Low-dimensional manifold, controlled: kernel ridge on noise-isotropic (unscaled) PCA scores vs P-004's standardized PCA

With scaler=none, the leading 24 PCs of the raw features are signal-dominated and the discarded directions are mostly noise. An RBF kernel ridge on these scores, with log target, should reach val rel_l2 < 0.06 and below P-004's standardized-PCA run at identical alpha and gamma_mult. Standardizing first lets noise-floor features rotate noise into the leading PCs.

If unscaled PCA with KRR matches the MLP, the inverse map is a smooth 4-D interpolation problem and the remaining effort should go to denoising rather than capacity. It pairs with the revised P-005 to form a 2x2 design: {MLP, KRR} x {standardized, noise-isotropic}.

PCA is applied after the scaler, so with scaler=none it acts on raw features.

The gamma 'scale' heuristic, applied to unscaled PC scores, is dominated by PC1's variance. gamma_mult=1.0 is a reasonable starting point but may oversmooth along low-variance PCs.
All splits come from the same simulator and noise model.

Signed sqrt amplifies noise near zero, so the sqrt arm is dropped.
The mean-baseline val rel_l2 is 0.3307.

P-017.author: researcher-experimental
P-017.title: Estimator-target alignment control: MSE on raw k (posterior-mean estimator) vs MSE on log k for the same MLP
P-017.hypothesis: rel_l2 is a squared-error metric in k-space. An MLP trained with MSE on untransformed k approximates the posterior mean E[k|data], which is the MMSE estimator under the uniform box prior. A log-target MLP approximates exp(E[log k|data]), which is biased low by about Var/2 wherever the posterior is wide. The predicted wide-posterior region is the outer segments and parameters near the bounds. The same architecture with target_transform='none' should therefore achieve val rel_l2 no worse than the log-target P-003, and should be at least 5% better on k1/k4 if those components are weakly identified.
P-017.motivation: Every active MLP proposal uses log targets, so there is no control for the target transform. The critic notes that if outer-sensor signal is weak, posterior-mean shrinkage becomes the relevant lever. Raw-k MSE training gives that shrinkage directly, without a forward model. The test is a clean single-factor ablation against P-003. It can distinguish two explanations of residual error: a transform-induced estimator bias, versus an information limit that no transform fixes.
assumptions: rel_l2 is computed in original k units, as ||k_hat - k|| / ||k|| aggregated over val, so it rewards the conditional mean.
The bounds [0.5, 2.0] span only a factor of 4, so raw-k targets are well-scaled and the network does not need log for numerical conditioning.
Positivity is not at risk, because the posterior mean lies inside the convex box. Any rare boundary overshoot is negligible relative to the metric.
The splits share a simulator and noise model.

evidence.claim: For a lognormal-like posterior with log-variance s^2, exp(E[log k]) = E[k]*exp(-s^2/2). The relative bias is about s^2/2, which matters for weakly identified components with s ~ 0.2-0.3.

If all components are tightly identified at sigma=1e-3 (s << 0.05), the two targets give near-identical estimators. The log target may then win slightly through better relative weighting of errors at small k.
The mean-baseline val rel_l2 is 0.3307.

citations.note: Identifiability heuristic only, since the coefficient regularity and data type do not match. Nothing about the estimator choice depends on it.

P-017.falsifiable_test: Refuted if val rel_l2 is worse than P-003's by more than the seed-to-seed spread, using a paired bootstrap 95% CI on the val difference that excludes 0 in P-003's favour. The k1/k4 sub-claim is refuted if the per-component relative error improvement on k1/k4 is under 5%, or not larger than the improvement on k2/k3. A null result, with both targets within the CI, means components are tightly identified and transform bias is negligible.

feasibility.notes: Same cost as P-003, about 30-60 s on CPU.

P-017.if_fails: If log clearly wins, either the log reparametrisation improves learnability of the inverse map (P-007's claim), or the metric is not pure squared error in k. Either way, log targets become the default. If there is no difference, posteriors are narrow and the remaining error is an approximation or capacity issue rather than an estimator-choice issue, which points effort at preprocessing (revised P-005/P-006) or ensembling.

P-018.hypothesis: With the P-003 MLP configuration held fixed, training on k (target_transform='none') gives val rel_l2 less than or equal to the log-target version. The gap concentrates on the weakly observed segments k1 and k4, where the Jensen bias exp(E[log k]) <= E[k] is largest. Both versions reach rel_l2 <= 0.05 only if posterior widths are small, i.e. if the outer sensors carry signal well above sigma.
P-018.motivation: Every active MLP proposal uses log targets. That is a framing assumption that no one has tested. Under a uniform prior in k and a squared-error metric, MSE on k is the Bayes-consistent estimand. MSE on log k estimates a geometric-mean-type quantity with downward bias of roughly Var_post(log k)*k/2. This experiment cleanly separates the 'conditioning' benefit claimed for log space from the 'estimand' cost of using it.

noise_scale=1e-3 is interpreted in raw feature units (equal to sigma) or smaller; it never exceeds sigma under any plausible semantics
P-003 is run with the same seed and architecture, so the comparison is paired
Posterior widths for k1/k4 are non-negligible; otherwise both estimands coincide and the ablation shows no difference, which is still informative

If neither reaches 0.05 and the k1/k4 errors dominate, the bottleneck is identifiability (signal at the outer sensors) rather than parametrisation. In that case the posterior mean (MSE on k) is the correct target for the final model.

P-019.author: researcher-exploratory
P-019.title: Merged P-002/P-008: forward surrogate + sigma-weighted, anchored, holdout-gated per-sample inversion
P-019.hypothesis: A 4-to-D MLP forward surrogate trained on the simulations reaches held-out residual RMSE rho <= 2 sigma (noise included, so rho ~ 1 is the ideal). When it does, refining the encoder's estimate by minimising ||(f(z)-x)/s_eff||^2 + anchor*||z-z0||^2 lowers rel_l2 by at least 10% relative to the encoder alone, and gives at least a 10% improvement over the best direct library regressor. If rho >> 2, refinement gives no gain and the gate disables it.
P-019.motivation: This challenges the framing that 'no forward model' implies pure inverse regression. The forward map of a parabolic PDE from 4 parameters is smooth and low-dimensional, so it is easier to learn than the inverse. Using it at test time enforces data consistency for each sample. Weighting by effective noise and anchoring to the encoder turn the procedure into an approximate MAP estimate under a learned, data-centred prior.
assumptions: Training features already contain sigma=1e-3 noise, so the ideal held-out surrogate RMSE in sigma units is ~1
Surrogate error can be modelled as extra i.i.d. Gaussian noise, so s_eff = sigma*max(1, rho)
The misfit is locally well behaved near the encoder guess; Adam with box projection in standardised log-k is enough
Losing 10% of the training data to the internal holdout costs less than the gate gains

evidence.claim: The forward solution is unique for a positive divergence-form coefficient, so the forward map is a well-defined function of k and is learnable.
With 3000 samples in 4-D, the surrogate error may exceed sigma across ~hundreds of output features. The gate and the s_eff inflation are designed for exactly this case.
If the encoder is already near the CRB, refinement can only add surrogate bias; the gate should then select the encoder.

citations.note: The positive coefficient and divergence-form diffusion match. The theorem is stated on R^n without boundaries, but forward uniqueness for 1-D homogeneous Dirichlet is standard. It gives no inverse identifiability or stability.

P-019.falsifiable_test: Primary: val rel_l2 is at least 10% below the best direct library regressor (P-003 or best KRR). Internal ablation: run the same spec with steps=0 (encoder only, same 90% training subset and seed). The refinement hypothesis fails if the refined run is less than 10% better than steps=0. Diagnostics to log: rho (surrogate held-out RMSE in sigma units) and use_ref. Read rho alongside the outcome: rho <= 2 with no gain falsifies the 'data consistency helps' claim; rho >> 2 with no gain points to surrogate capacity or sample size instead.

feasibility.notes: Two 3-layer MLPs at 120 epochs on 2700 and 5400 rows, plus two 200-step batched Adam refinements (holdout of 300, val of 750). Estimated 60-120 s on CPU. Drop epochs to 80 if over budget.

P-019.if_fails: If rho >> 2, a generic MLP cannot learn the forward map to noise accuracy from 3000 samples. The next step would be a structured surrogate, e.g. a PCA basis of traces with coefficients smooth in log k, or a parametrisation by eigen-decay rates. If rho ~ 1 but refinement still does not help, the direct inverse regressor is already near the information limit. Remaining error is then posterior width, and effort should move to estimand choice (P-007) rather than model capacity.

P-020.title: Noise-isotropic raw-unit PCA (CV-chosen cutoff, whiten vs Wiener weighting, m<=64) + median-bandwidth RBF kernel ridge, log-k target
P-020.hypothesis: When the PCA front end is chosen by inner holdout on train only (cutoff factor, whitening vs Wiener-like spectral weighting, m capped at 64), an RBF kernel ridge on the scores reaches val rel_l2 within 1.15x of P-003's full-fidelity MLP and below 0.05. Failure with the MLP succeeding implies the inverse map needs an adaptive (k-aligned) metric. Failure with both models tied above 0.05 is evidence of an information floor.
P-020.motivation: The pilot KRR's 1.26x gap may come from metric flaws (standardization breaking noise isotropy, fixed PCA24, a fixed bandwidth), not from KRR's inability to represent a smooth map on a 4-D manifold. Making the spectral weighting and cutoff data-selected, and capping dimension, isolates that question. Because the map is low-dimensional, a GP-mean-like smoother is a strong nonparametric reference against which to judge the MLP.
assumptions: Raw features carry i.i.d. N(0, 1e-6) noise, so raw-unit PCA eigenvalues are signal variance plus sigma^2 (approximately, since the signal is nonlinear in k)
At most 64 noise-floor-clearing components carry the usable k information
One isotropic RBF bandwidth on spectrally weighted scores is adequate. This is not k-adapted and is a known limitation
A single 2:1 train-only holdout selects hyperparameters reliably enough (1000 holdout rows)
The exp(log-prediction) bias is small for well-identified components

evidence.claim: Pilot KRR (standardized, PCA24) reached 0.0679 vs the MLP's 0.0539 at n=300, a 1.26x ratio
In raw units the noise is isotropic, so the eigenvalue noise floor sigma^2 is identifiable
Wiener-like weighting shrinks components with low signal-to-noise ratio, avoiding the noise amplification of full whitening

P-022.author: researcher-experimental
P-022.title: Measurement preprocessing test: noise-isotropic (unscaled) PCA front end vs per-feature standardization for the log-k MLP
P-022.hypothesis: Per-feature standardization amplifies near-noise-floor features, mainly early-time readings at the outer sensors (indices 5 and 35). This raises the effective noise the MLP has to learn to ignore. If the raw features are left unscaled, the additive noise stays i.i.d. and isotropic. Projecting onto the leading 32 principal components then keeps the signal subspace and discards most noise energy. The same MLP on this representation should reach val rel_l2 below 0.9x that of the standardized-raw MLP (P-003). The gain should be largest for k1 and k4.
P-022.motivation: This is a measurement-design question: how should the sensor time series be weighted before regression? Under i.i.d. Gaussian noise the noise-whitened metric is the raw Euclidean one. Standardization distorts that metric in favour of features with low marginal variance, and these are exactly the features with the lowest SNR. Unscaled PCA is the classical optimal linear denoiser for isotropic noise. The proposal differs from P-003 only in scaler and PCA, so the comparison is a controlled single-factor ablation.
assumptions: Features are raw noisy temperatures in the same units as sigma=1e-3, so the noise is isotropic in raw feature space.
The harness applies PCA after the scaler. With scaler=none, PCA therefore acts on raw features.
The torch_mlp's LayerNorm makes it insensitive to the overall scale of the PCA scores, which are not standardized.
32 components capture the signal manifold. The intrinsic dimension is 4, but the map is curved, so more linear components than 4 are needed.

P-024.author: researcher-experimental
P-024.title: Estimator-target alignment control: MSE on raw k (posterior-mean estimator) vs MSE on log k for the same MLP
P-024.hypothesis: rel_l2 is a squared-error metric in k-space. An MLP trained with MSE on untransformed k approximates the posterior mean E[k|data], which is the MMSE estimator under the uniform box prior. A log-target MLP approximates exp(E[log k|data]), which is biased low by about Var/2 wherever the posterior is wide. The predicted wide-posterior region is the outer segments and parameters near the bounds. The same architecture with target_transform='none' should therefore achieve val rel_l2 no worse than the log-target P-003, and should be at least 5% better on k1/k4 if those components are weakly identified.
P-024.motivation: Every active MLP proposal uses log targets, so there is no control for the target transform. The critic notes that if outer-sensor signal is weak, posterior-mean shrinkage becomes the relevant lever. Raw-k MSE training gives that shrinkage directly, without a forward model. The test is a clean single-factor ablation against P-003. It can distinguish two explanations of residual error: a transform-induced estimator bias, versus an information limit that no transform fixes.
assumptions: rel_l2 is computed in original k units, as ||k_hat - k|| / ||k|| aggregated over val, so it rewards the conditional mean.
The bounds [0.5, 2.0] span only a factor of 4, so raw-k targets are well-scaled and the network does not need log for numerical conditioning.
Positivity is not at risk, because the posterior mean lies inside the convex box. Any rare boundary overshoot is negligible relative to the metric.

Recast it as an equivalence test: |Δ rel_l2| < 3% relative, with a 95% paired CI. Separately, the k1/k4 signed bias of the log model should be negative and larger in magnitude than that of the raw model.

evidence.claim: For a lognormal-like posterior with log-variance s^2, exp(E[log k]) = E[k]*exp(-s^2/2). The relative bias is about s^2/2, which matters for weakly identified components with s ~ 0.2-0.3.

If all components are tightly identified at sigma=1e-3 (s << 0.05), the two targets give near-identical estimators. The log target may then win slightly through better relative weighting of errors at small k.

P-025.title: Surviving surrogate spec: learned forward net + per-feature-variance chi² refinement, encoder-calibrated anchor, paired hold-out gate (absorbs P-010)
P-025.hypothesis: An MLP forward surrogate (log k → standardised traces) trained on 2700 simulations reaches a hold-out per-feature residual RMS of rho ≤ 2·sigma, noise included. When it does, minimising a per-feature-weighted chi² plus an encoder-calibrated Gaussian anchor lowers hold-out and val rel_l2 by ≥10% relative to the same encoder with steps=0. P-025.motivation: This challenges the 'no forward model ⇒ pure inverse regression' framing. The 4→D forward map of a parabolic PDE is smooth and low-dimensional, so learning it is easier than learning the inverse. A per-sample data-consistency step can then remove the encoder's regression-to-the-mean bias, which is largest on the weakly informed outer segments. Calibrating both the noise model (per-feature v_j) and the prior (encoder hold-out RMSE) from data, rather than hand-tuning them, makes this an approximate MAP under a learned likelihood and a data-centred prior.

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def _mlp(i,o,h=256):
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(i,h),nn.SiLU(),nn.Linear(h,h),nn.SiLU(),nn.Linear(h,h),nn.SiLU(),nn.Linear(h,o))

def _train(net,a,b,E,lr=2e-3,bs=128,noise=None):
    opt=torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(),lr=lr)
    sch=torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt,max(E,1))
    n=a.shape[0]
    for ep in range(E):
        perm=torch.randperm(n)
        for i in range(0,n,bs):
            idx=perm[i:i+bs]
            xb=a[idx]
            if noise is not None:
                xb=xb+torch.randn_like(xb)*noise
            loss=((net(xb)-b[idx])**2).mean()
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        sch.step()
    net.eval()
    return net

class SurrogateInvert:
    def fit(self,X,y):
        p=self.p
        torch.manual_seed(self.seed)
        X=np.asarray(X,dtype=float); y=np.asarray(y,dtype=float)
        sig=float(p.get('sigma',1e-3))
        self.xm=X.mean(0); self.xs=X.std(0)+1e-8
        t=np.log(np.clip(y,1e-6,None)); self.tm=t.mean(0); self.ts=t.std(0)+1e-8
        Xt=torch.tensor((X-self.xm)/self.xs,dtype=torch.float32)
        Tt=torch.tensor((t-self.tm)/self.ts,dtype=torch.float32)
        n=X.shape[0]; perm=np.random.RandomState(self.seed).permutation(n)
        nh=max(int(0.1*n),50); ho=torch.tensor(perm[:nh]); tr=torch.tensor(perm[nh:])
        d=X.shape[1]; E=int(p.get('epochs',100))
        xs_t=torch.tensor(self.xs,dtype=torch.float32)
        self.f=_train(_mlp(4,d),Tt[tr],Xt[tr],E)
        self.g=_train(_mlp(d,4),Xt[tr],Tt[tr],E,noise=sig/xs_t)
        for q in self.f.parameters(): q.requires_grad_(False)
        for q in self.g.parameters(): q.requires_grad_(False)
        with torch.no_grad():
            r=(self.f(Tt[ho])-Xt[ho])*xs_t
            v=torch.clamp(r.pow(2).mean(0),min=sig*sig)
            self.rho=float(v.mean().sqrt())/sig
            self.w=xs_t/v.sqrt()
            e=(self.g(Xt[ho])-Tt[ho]).pow(2).mean(0).sqrt()
            self.prec=1.0/torch.clamp(e,min=1e-3).pow(2)
        self.lo=torch.tensor((np.log(0.5)-self.tm)/self.ts,dtype=torch.float32)
        self.hi=torch.tensor((np.log(2.0)-self.tm)/self.ts,dtype=torch.float32)
        self.use=False; self.gate=(0.0,0.0)
        if int(p.get('steps',200))>0:
            yh=y[perm[:nh]]
            e0=self._err(self._k(self._enc(Xt[ho])),yh)
            e1=self._err(self._k(self._refine(Xt[ho])),yh)
            self.gate=(e0,e1)
            self.use=bool(e1<0.98*e0)
        return self

    def _err(self,K,Y):
        return float(np.linalg.norm(K-Y)/np.linalg.norm(Y))

    def _k(self,z):
        return np.clip(np.exp(z.numpy()*self.ts+self.tm),0.5,2.0)

    def _enc(self,Xt):
        with torch.no_grad():
            return self.g(Xt)

    def _refine(self,Xt):
        z0=torch.max(torch.min(self._enc(Xt),self.hi),self.lo)
        z=z0.clone().requires_grad_(True)
        opt=torch.optim.Adam([z],lr=float(self.p.get('lr_inv',0.01)))
        a=float(self.p.get('anchor',1.0))
        for s in range(int(self.p.get('steps',200))):
            res=(self.f(z)-Xt)*self.w
            loss=0.5*res.pow(2).sum()+0.5*a*((z-z0).pow(2)*self.prec).sum()
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
            with torch.no_grad():
                z.copy_(torch.max(torch.min(z,self.hi),self.lo))
        return z.detach()

    def predict(self,X):
        Xt=torch.tensor((np.asarray(X,dtype=float)-self.xm)/self.xs,dtype=torch.float32)
        z=self._refine(Xt) if self.use else self._enc(Xt)
        return self._k(z)

def build_model(params,task,seed):
    m=SurrogateInvert()
    m.p=dict(params)
    m.seed=int(seed)
    return m
